name: Repository certification
description: Research data repositories use certification to demonstrate that they meet recognized standards for data quality, security, preservation, and accessibility. It promotes transparency and accountability by providing an independent assessment of a repository’s policies, processes, and infrastructure.
markdownContent:
#### Sections
[What is repository certification?](#what-is-repository-certification) | [Why is repository certification important?](#why-is-repo-certification-important) | [Authors](#authors)

### What is repository certification?

Researchers, data stewards, funders and other stakeholders need a framework of internationally recognised certification standards for digital repositories in order to assess and improve the quality of their work processes and management systems. A term often used in this respect is [Trustworthy Digital Repository](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-28032-0_42) (TDR) which is  referring to repositories that ensure long-term preservation, accessibility, and reuse of research outputs. In the European Framework for Audit and Certification of Digital Repositories three kinds of certification with increasing degrees of complexity and depth are available:

* [CoreTrustSeal](https://www.coretrustseal.org/) (CTS): this is based on [Data Seal of Approval](https://phys-techsciences.datastations.nl/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.17026/dans-28z-njxq) (DSA) and [World Data System](https://worlddatasystem.org/) (WDS) and represents the most widely adopted certification, focusing on core requirements such as data integrity, accessibility, and sustainability. Certified digital repositories are listed at [CTS](https://amt.coretrustseal.org/certificates). 
* [Nestor Seal](https://www.langzeitarchivierung.de/Webs/nestor/EN/Home/home_node.html): verification according to DIN 31644 
* [ISO 16363 certification](https://www.iso.org/standard/87472.html): formal level certification

The assessments vary in intensity from a peer review of completed documentation (self-assessment) to a prepared on-site visit by an external audit team. These instruments are used worldwide. Data sponsors, producers and re-users may trust any managing body that has been certified according to one of the above standards.

### Why is repository certification important?

[CTS](http://www.coretrustseal.org/why-certification/): "If we want to be able to share data, we need to store them in a trustworthy data repository. Data created and used by scientists should be managed, curated, and archived in such a way to preserve the initial investment in collecting them. Researchers must be certain that data held in archives remain useful and meaningful into the future. Funding authorities increasingly require continued access to data produced by the projects they fund, and have made this an important element in Data Management Plans. Indeed, some funders now stipulate that the data they fund must be deposited in a trustworthy repository."


### Authors

name: Enabling discovery and identification
description: To facilitate reuse of data, we need to first make data discoverable. Data discoverability involves assigning identifiers and metadata to a dataset to allow users to query, find, interpret, and reuse it. Choosing an appropriate repository, improving file structure, providing documentation, and producing machine-discoverable metadata, are all part of this process. Making data discoverable also contributes to making research more transparent and reproducible.

name: Preparing deposits - file formats and technical data quality
description: Considering data preservation and reusability during preparation helps ensure that the dataset remains accessible, understandable, and usable beyond the original research project. Good preparation—such as using sustainable formats, documenting data structures, and recording processing steps—reduces the risk of data becoming inaccessible, ambiguous, or unusable over time. It also makes it easier for other researchers to verify, reproduce, and build on the research.

[Considerations](#conciderations) | [Recommandations](#recommandations) | [More information](#more-information) | [Authors](#authors)

### Considerations
Key aspects to consider include:
- Did you review the data you plan to deposit (e.g. are all necessary files included/unnecessary or redundant files removed? Which are raw, processed, derived, or final data?)  
- Are the file formats appropriate (e.g. widely used and supported, non-proprietary if possible)?
- Is technical file quality (e.g. files open correctly, completeness, coherent and clear file names) ok?
- Is the data machine-readable (e.g. consistent data types, consistent representations of missing values,  include units of measurement)?
- Did you use documented standards and conventions (e.g. units, geographic coordinates and reference systems, variable names and identifiers) commonly used in your scientific discipline?
- Is the data internally consistent (e.g. consistent variable names)?
- Is the data sufficiently and clearly explained and documented (e.g. readme file)?
- Did you include provenance and processing information (e.g. processing scripts/documentation)?
- Does the metadata reflect the actual files?


### Recommandations
- Check and follow the deposit guidelines of the repository you chose for your data deposit
- Familiarise yourself with (meta)data standards as well as conventions within your discipline and use them consistently
- Think about future re-use: does the dataset contain all necessary information by someone else?


### More information
